statement: OpenAI said on 2026-08-17 that it agreed to secure up to roughly 8 GW of capacity at the Pike County complex, with the first 800 MW expected online by 2028.
account: The instruction I applied was: “A statement bears on a question when its figure or fact changes what that question’s answer will be.” I considered v31, which takes NVIDIA’s binding guarantee or backstop for OpenAI’s Ohio lease or construction debt, and rejected it because e2 reports OpenAI securing capacity, not an NVIDIA backstop. I also considered v33, which takes NVIDIA’s binding financing obligation for OpenAI data centers, and rejected it because e2 states OpenAI’s capacity agreement and expected timing, not an NVIDIA financing obligation.

statement: Wall Street analysts expected NVIDIA growth of 82% for the rest of 2026; the article does not specify the underlying financial measure.
account: The instruction was: “A statement bears on a question when its figure or fact changes what that question’s answer will be.” I considered v2 and rejected it because “82% growth” does not specify total revenue or a direct driver of total revenue; I considered v6 and rejected it because it does not specify gross margin or a direct driver of gross margin. The statement says only that analysts expect NVIDIA growth, without identifying the financial measure, so it does not change either answer.

statement: Recent U.S. approvals had cleared around 10 Chinese firms to receive advanced AI hardware from NVIDIA and AMD by July 15, 2026.
account: The relevant instruction is: “A statement bears on a question when its figure or fact changes what that question’s answer will be”; e3 reports U.S. approvals, not Chinese government action. I should have considered and rejected v3 and v11 because neither says China permitted H200 sales or authorized imports. The same reason applies to v14: e3 does not report Chinese government permission for selected companies to purchase H200 chips.
